rationale:
No radar item qualifies for Lane C today. Elecoglipron's new study is from Oct 19, efpeglenatide's launch is expected around Oct 29, and CagriSema has no FDA decision yet. So the long-form follows playbook priority 2: a Lane P 'What Is [drug]?' decoder on elecoglipron. It's a brand-new, under-covered drug name (the EloraTZP pattern). It rests on primary sources that can be checked in depth: the Lancet Phase 2b VISTA paper (June 2026), the Br J Clin Pharmacol fed vs fasted study (Oct 19) and ClinicalTrials.gov Phase 3 records. That fits the long-form fact-check rule. It ends by naming the live Orforglipron long-form.

I skipped Lane A 'what happens when you stop' because the 09-29 long-form and the 10-13 and 10-19 pieces cover that ground inside the 30-day window. I skipped the muscle and SURMOUNT-1 body-scan Shorts and the TRIUMPH-OSA Short because of the variety guard: those trials were used 10-21, 10-23 and 10-24.

The Shorts follow the playbook slots:
- 08:00: a calm honest-uncertainty body-worry Short on the tirzepatide gallbladder trial data (the top Instagram format, tirzepatide in the title).
- 13:00: a tirzepatide-named benefit question hooked on the new Oct 12 EClinicalMedicine meta-regression on blood pressure.
- 20:00: a funnel spin-off of today's L1. It asks one fresh question the long-form answers (the food rules, from the Oct 19 fed vs fasted study), not a re-cut. The CTA names L1's exact live title once the oEmbed check passes; otherwise it says 'follow for more'.

The carousel reuses verified Short text only, per the playbook. It comes from the 10-23 semaglutide grip-strength Short, which shipped and reached 139 on Instagram. Drop it if that script isn't confirmed as verified.

Mix: 3 emerging or rising pieces (L1, S2, S3), 1 evergreen refresh (S1), 1 reuse (C1) with a myth-correcting angle.

Body systems vary: drug pharmacology for L1 and S3, the gallbladder for S1, blood pressure for S2, muscle strength for C1.

Pillars: research, get-the-most ×2, beyond-weight, how-it-works.

Nothing uses a reject topic, cost, gray-market or 'approved yet?' framing.

pieces.topic: Elecoglipron (AstraZeneca), an investigational once-daily small-molecule GLP-1 pill: how it works, what the VISTA Phase 2b trial showed (Lancet, June 2026: 310 adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition; 11.8% average weight loss at 36 weeks on the 75 mg arm vs 0.3% on placebo), the new fed vs fasted study (Br J Clin Pharmacol, Oct 19, 2026, healthy volunteers), and its dated Phase 3 status
pieces.angle:
Lane P decoder (log 'lane: P'), series 'New GLP-1 Drug Decoded'. 0–15 s: what viewers will know by the end, the first answer ('a once-daily GLP-1 pill that's still investigational, now in Phase 3') and a dated status. Chapters named as searched questions:
(1) What is elecoglipron?
(2) How is a small-molecule pill different from a peptide like oral semaglutide, and why does oral semaglutide have food and water rules? Cite the label wording.
(3) What did the Phase 2 trial show? Per-arm results vs placebo, group sizes, the estimand and 36 weeks, copied from the Lancet paper; the population stated exactly.
(4) Blood sugar results, only if the paper reports them, with the population for each.
(5) Side effects: GI rates per arm vs placebo and discontinuations, from the paper.
(6) Can you take it with food? What the fed vs fasted study measured. Healthy volunteers, Phase 1, pharmacokinetics only, not a weight result.
(7) Where it sits next to oral semaglutide and orforglipron: separate trials, not head-to-head, no ranking.
(8) What's next: Phase 3 trial names and dates from ClinicalTrials.gov or AstraZeneca releases. Investigational, not approved by the FDA, MHRA, Health Canada or TGA as of 26 Oct 2026.
No 'beat' frame. Re-hook every 45–75 s. One subscribe ask, after the trial payoff. Never online sources; for approved options or a clinical trial, ask a prescriber. Include 'Not personal advice', 'don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own' and the full prescriber line. End by naming the live long-form 'Orforglipron (Foundayo): The GLP-1 Pill With No Food Rules (US Label)'. 8–12 min, 14:00 ET.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide and the gallbladder: how often gallbladder problems (gallstones, gallbladder inflammation) were reported in the SURMOUNT-1 trial, why rapid weight loss raises gallstone risk, and the warning signs on the label
pieces.angle: Gallbladder problems were uncommon in the trial data. Gallstones were reported at a similar rate on tirzepatide and placebo (about 1 in 100). Gallbladder inflammation was less common, but it showed up more on tirzepatide (0.7% vs 0.2%). Quote the exact source (the NEJM SURMOUNT-1 supplement or the label) and its population, 'without diabetes'. Then: fast weight loss by any method is linked to gallstones. Give the label's warning signs and 'tell your healthcare provider right away'. Add 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own', 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide and Your Gallbladder: How Common Are Problems?
pieces.why: The playbook's 08:00 body-worry slot (our top Instagram format) with tirzepatide in the title. The evidence is settled trial and label data, and gallbladder hasn't been covered in the last 30 days. | fact-check: The figures the label reports don't support 'more frequent on tirzepatide' as a blanket claim. Cholelithiasis (gallstones) was about 1.1% on tirzepatide vs 1.0% on placebo, which is essentially similar. Cholecystitis (gallbladder inflammation) was 0.7% vs 0.2%, and cholecystectomy 0.2% vs 0%. The label figures may be pooled across trials, so either take per-arm SURMOUNT-1 numbers from the NEJM 2022 supplement or say 'in the Zepbound label's trial data'. Don't present pooled figures as SURMOUNT-1. The label's urgency wording is 'tell your healthcare provider right away'. Use that word for word, with the four symptoms (upper-stomach pain, fever, yellowing of skin or eyes, clay-colored stools). Source: https://medical.lilly.com/us/products/answers/can-people-with-gallbladder-disease-or-gallbladder-removal-take-zepbound-tirzepatide-266122

pieces.topic: Does tirzepatide lower blood pressure? A new meta-regression of Phase 3 trials of GLP-1 and multi-hormone drugs in adults with overweight or obesity (EClinicalMedicine, Oct 12, 2026)
pieces.angle: Does tirzepatide lower blood pressure? In SURMOUNT-1 (adults with obesity or overweight without diabetes, 72 weeks), systolic blood pressure fell more on tirzepatide than on placebo. Quote the exact NEJM mmHg figures. Then the bigger picture: a pooled analysis of 32 Phase 3 obesity-drug trials found blood pressure fell more where weight fell more (about 0.34 mmHg per 1% of weight lost). That's 'linked to', pooled data, not head-to-head, and blood pressure wasn't the trials' main goal. Cite it by its verified publication (otherwise as the ECO May 2026 analysis). Add 'Never change your blood pressure medicines on your own; review lower readings with your doctor', one GI line, 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: Does Tirzepatide Lower Blood Pressure? New Trial Analysis
pieces.why: Tirzepatide-first titles are our proven Shorts format (median 102). This is a fresh peer-reviewed meta-regression on a searched beyond-weight question, with little video coverage. | fact-check: I couldn't confirm an EClinicalMedicine paper dated 12 Oct 2026. The only version I could verify is the European Congress on Obesity abstract (EurekAlert, 14 May 2026): 32 Phase 3 trials, 43,618 adults with overweight or obesity, a pooled −10.9% placebo-adjusted weight loss and −5.2 mmHg systolic, and about 0.34 mmHg less systolic pressure per 1% of weight lost. It gives NO figure for tirzepatide alone. Its stated caveat: blood pressure wasn't a primary outcome, and changes to background blood pressure medicines may have affected the results. So the tirzepatide answer has to come from SURMOUNT-1 (NEJM 2022, week 72, versus placebo, population without diabetes). Copy that figure exactly from the paper. Cite the meta-analysis only by its confirmed published record (journal, date, DOI). If the scriptwriter can't find it, call it the 'May 2026 European Congress on Obesity analysis'. Add a safety line: people on blood pressure medicines can get readings that run low; discuss it with your doctor. Source: https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1128310

pieces.topic: Can you take elecoglipron with food? The Oct 19, 2026 Phase 1 fed vs fasted study in healthy volunteers, and why oral semaglutide has food and water rules
pieces.angle: 20:00 funnel spin-off of L1 (Exp D). It asks one fresh question rather than re-cutting the long-form. Answer within 10 s: what the fed vs fasted study measured (drug levels in the blood with and without food), in healthy volunteers, as the abstract words it. Not a weight result and not a label instruction. One line: oral semaglutide is a peptide and its label has food and water timing rules ('follow your label'); elecoglipron is a small molecule. One dated status line: investigational, in Phase 3, not approved anywhere as of 26 Oct 2026. One GI line from the Phase 2 trial. For approved options or a trial, ask a prescriber. 'Not personal advice' plus the full prescriber line. Last spoken line: 'Full breakdown: [L1's exact live title], on our channel.' L1's URL goes on description line 1 and in the pinned comment, only after the oEmbed check confirms it opens L1; otherwise say 'follow for more' and don't count it toward Exp D. 170 words or fewer. Mix at masking 0.02 or lower.

pieces.angle:
Minimum-effort carousel built only from the verified 10-23 Short script, with no new research. Drop it if that script isn't confirmed as verified.
Slides:
(1) The worry, named as understandable.
(2) 10 pooled studies, 660 people on semaglutide: no clear change in average handgrip strength, exactly as verified.
(3) Very low certainty and studies that varied a lot.
(4) Lean mass (weight) is not the same as strength (function).
(5) The SURMOUNT-1 body-scan anchor (tirzepatide; adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes; 72 weeks), exactly as verified.
(6) Recommended habits, not proven on the drug: a protein food at each meal unless your clinician has told you to limit protein (for example, kidney disease), and muscle-strengthening at least 2 days a week, started gently.
(7) Common GI side effects, 'don't stop or change your medicines on your own', 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line.
No emoji.
